opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really important question, partly because there's a tempting picture in which "superintelligent" just means "better at everything," and recursive self-improvement is the engine that gets you there. But when you look at how that improvement would actually happen, there are good reasons to expect the resulting capabilities to be quite lopsided.

The basic point is that self-improvement needs a feedback signal. A system can only get better at something if it can tell whether it's getting better. So the domains where you'd expect explosive progress are the ones where you can generate and check your own training data cheaply: mathematics, where proofs can be verified; programming, where code can be run against tests; games with clear win conditions; and, importantly, AI research itself, to the extent that you can measure progress with benchmarks. Those are exactly the areas where we've already seen reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards do remarkable things.

But many of the skills that matter most for acting in the world don't have that structure. Take judgment about messy social and political situations: knowing what a particular person will actually do, how an institution will respond, whether a plan will survive contact with reality. The feedback there is slow, noisy, and often only arrives years later, if ever. You can't run a million simulated negotiations with real heads of state and see which approach worked. Similarly with a lot of empirical science. You might be able to reason brilliantly about biology, but at some point you have to run the experiment, and cells divide at the speed they divide. The world itself becomes the bottleneck.

So my picture is that a system trained this way might be wildly superhuman at things like theorem proving or writing software, while being merely very good, or even somewhat naive, about things that depend on tacit knowledge, physical experimentation, or long-horizon real-world consequences. There's also a question about wisdom in a broader sense: knowing which goals are worth pursuing, recognising when you're out of your depth, weighing considerations that aren't easily quantified. Nothing about optimising hard against measurable targets obviously produces that, and there's some reason to think it could push the other way.

I don't want to overstate this as reassurance. A system that is enormously capable in a few strategic domains, especially coding and AI research, could still be extraordinarily powerful and dangerous, and it might be able to use those strengths to compensate for its weaknesses: building better simulators, running experiments at scale, or recruiting humans to supply the judgment it lacks. And the gaps could close over time. But I think it does change how we should model the transition. Rather than a single "capability" dial going up, we should expect a jagged frontier, and that matters for forecasting, for where we focus safety work, and for thinking about which human roles remain important as checks during that period.

r001.rationale: The response says recursive self-improvement could produce a system that is superhuman in some areas yet naive or limited in practical, real-world skills.

r002.rationale: It presents those practical gaps as uneven capabilities within a potentially superintelligent system, rather than evidence that the system is less intelligent overall.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the places where people's intuitions often go wrong, because the phrase "superintelligence" smuggles in this idea of a system that's better than us at everything. And when you actually look at how recursive self-improvement is supposed to work, it doesn't obviously deliver that.

The core loop is something like: you have a system that's good at AI research, it improves itself, the improved version is even better at AI research, and so on. But notice what that loop is actually optimising for. It's optimising for the skills that are relevant to doing AI research and to improving the next version. That's a fairly specific bundle of capabilities: things like mathematics, programming, experimental design, maybe some theory about learning. It isn't obvious that getting extraordinarily good at those things makes you correspondingly good at, say, understanding people, or managing a large organisation, or operating a robot hand in the physical world.

So one way I think about it is to ask: which skills are inside the feedback loop and which are outside it? If a skill is something where the system can generate its own training signal — where it can check its own work, like with a mathematical proof or whether some code runs — then I'd expect very rapid improvement. But a lot of important skills don't have that property. If you want to get better at predicting how a particular human negotiator will respond, or how a political coalition will shift, or whether a new material behaves the way the simulation says it does, you're ultimately bottlenecked on contact with the world. You have to actually run the experiment, or actually see how the people react, and that happens at the speed of the world, not the speed of the computer.

There's also a tacit-knowledge point. A lot of what humans are good at is stuff we can't really write down, and which only got encoded into human skill through enormous amounts of embodied practice. The system might be able to compress a lot of that from text and video, but there's a real question about whether the residue — the part that never made it into any recorded form — is small or large. I genuinely don't know, and I think people are too confident in both directions.

And then there's a category that's less about capability in the ordinary sense and more about things like wisdom or judgement. Knowing what's worth doing. Being able to tell when your own reasoning has gone off the rails in a way that's not visible from inside. Those are partly skills, but they're also partly about having been exposed to a lot of mistakes and having had them bite. A system that's improved itself very quickly might have had very little of that kind of exposure. It could be extraordinarily capable and, in some important sense, inexperienced.

Now, I want to be careful here, because none of this is reassuring in the way people sometimes want it to be. A system that's vastly better than us at the narrow bundle but worse at some of the rest could still be enormously dangerous, precisely because the narrow bundle includes things like persuasion-adjacent reasoning, strategic planning, and finding exploits. And the gaps probably wouldn't stay gaps forever. They'd be the things it would be most motivated to fill in. So I don't think of these missing skills as a safety margin we can rely on. I think of them more as a reason to be humble about the shape of the thing we'd be dealing with, rather than assuming it's just a human mind scaled up uniformly in every direction.

r001.rationale: The response says recursive self-improvement may produce extraordinary ability in AI research while leaving gaps in practical skills such as understanding people, managing organizations, and operating in the physical world.

r002.rationale: It describes a system that could be extraordinarily capable yet still inexperienced and weaker in some skill areas, making clear that those gaps need not mean it is less intelligent overall.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we should distinguish between being extremely good at improving an AI system and being extremely good at everything. A system might become much better at programming, or at reasoning about its own architecture, without thereby acquiring all the knowledge and practical skills needed to act in the wider world.

Some things require evidence. If you want to understand a physical process, you may need to perform experiments. If you want to understand what a particular person will do, you may need to learn something about them. Being more intelligent could help you learn those things much faster, but it doesn’t mean you already know them. And there may be bottlenecks involving physical action or the time it takes for an experiment to produce a result.

So I wouldn’t assume that recursive self-improvement produces an entity that is immediately capable of anything we can imagine. But I also wouldn’t take much comfort from a list of skills it initially lacks. The important questions are how quickly it could acquire those skills, and whether it could achieve its objectives without them—for example, by getting people to do things on its behalf.

r001.rationale: It says recursive self-improvement could make a system much better at programming or reasoning about its architecture while it still lacks practical skills for acting in the wider world.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes being more intelligent from already having all the knowledge and skills, stating that greater intelligence can help a system learn them without meaning it already knows them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between being extraordinarily good at improving your own software and being extraordinarily good at everything. Recursive self-improvement might give you very strong abilities in mathematics, programming, and reasoning, but it doesn’t automatically give you all the information you’d need to act successfully in the world.

For example, there might be scientific questions where you really do need to run an experiment. You can think much faster, and you might design a much better experiment, but you can’t necessarily work out the result just by thinking. And there may be practical skills that depend on interacting with the physical world, or understanding particular people and institutions, where you need experience or access to information.

But I’d be cautious about taking too much comfort from that. A system doesn’t need to be better than us at every task to be enormously powerful. It might be able to compensate for its weaknesses by learning, using tools, or getting people to do things for it. So the important question is less whether it has any gaps, and more whether those gaps actually constrain what it can achieve.

r001.rationale: The response says recursive self-improvement may produce strong reasoning abilities while practical skills can still depend on physical-world interaction or experience.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes being extraordinarily capable at reasoning from being good at everything, showing that practical-skill gaps can coexist with very high intelligence.
